demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
I remind myself it could have been worse
I dwell on what I have done wrong

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I feel isolated and set apart from others
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only markedly high-risk/impulsive strategy and is poorly supported by the rest of the selected nodes. The other strategies are comparatively cognitive/obsessional (mental rituals, downward comparison), and the threat/memory/appraisal items do not show the broader dysregulation, dissociation, or severe affective overload that would make this combination clinically cohesive.

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Pain recall implies the patient was physically injured in the traumatic event. That is hard to reconcile with the trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another' unless she was also injured, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. The rest of the memory items emphasize fragmented retrieval and sensory reliving, but not a personally injured trauma narrative.

vignette: Aisha, a 47-year-old architect, had always prided herself on her ability to visualize spaces and design efficiently. However, one fateful afternoon, while overseeing a construction site, a tragic accident occurred. A miscalculation on her part led to a scaffolding collapse that seriously injured a worker. The event replayed in her mind like a relentless loop; she could taste the dust that filled the air and hear the distant cries for help, sensations that suddenly returned to her whenever she tried to recall the incident. This vivid recall left Aisha feeling not only horrified but also deeply ashamed. She often found herself ruminating on the blunder, believing that someone else in her position would have acted differently. This constant self-blame led Aisha to develop various mental rituals, convinced that if she performed them, she might prevent anything bad from happening again. Her negative appraisals made her feel that these rituals were not merely habits, but essential acts of atonement that might somehow absolve her guilt and shield her from future mistakes. Aisha’s belief that she was responsible for the accident drove her to engage in these maladaptive strategies, reinforcing her negative view of herself. Each time she resorted to her rituals, she felt a quiet confirmation that she was fragile, further entrenching her negative appraisals. Each time she engaged in these rituals, she could not shake the belief that her inability to cope without them confirmed her fragility, deepening her conviction that she was somehow less than others who navigated life more easily. Her belief that she was responsible for the accident drove her to engage in these maladaptive strategies, as she thought they would somehow absolve her guilt and protect her from further harm. The weight of her self-blame was heavy, and she felt unrecognizable as the confident architect she once was. In the months that followed, Aisha's world began to shrink. She distanced herself from her colleagues and avoided social gatherings, feeling isolated and set apart from others who seemed to navigate life effortlessly. Every time she heard a loud noise, a sudden laugh, or even the whir of machinery, she would jump, her heart racing as if she were still at the construction site. Aisha had come to believe her life was now fraught with danger, and she often acted as though she was still in immediate peril, even when she was at home, surrounded by her family. When faced with this overwhelming sense of threat, it seemed only sensible to her to avoid certain environments and situations that might trigger her anxiety, allowing her world to grow smaller and more contained. The persistent feeling of danger made her avoidance strategies feel like necessary precautions, as if steering clear of potential triggers was the only way to maintain her safety and sanity. Her perception of danger felt so immediate that it led her to adopt avoidance strategies, as she thought steering clear of potential triggers was the only way to keep herself safe. The anxiety bled into her work, leaving her unable to concentrate on her designs or communicate effectively with her team. Each time she relied on these coping mechanisms, Aisha felt an unspoken message reinforcing that she was incapable of handling her responsibilities, deepening her negative self-perception. The resulting feelings of inadequacy would then spiral into a belief that she was a failure, which further fueled her anxiety and avoidance of professional interactions. Every time Aisha felt the need to employ these strategies, it left her with the insidious thought that her inability to cope without them confirmed her fragility, which only heightened the sense of threat she felt in her daily life. To cope, Aisha developed various mental rituals, convinced that if she performed them, she might prevent anything bad from happening again. However, these rituals paradoxically reinforced her memories, making them feel more potent and unmanageable, as if she had never truly put the event to rest. Each time she caught herself thinking about the accident, she would force herself to distract with thoughts of how things could have been worse — perhaps someone could have died. This attempt to manage her intrusive memories through distraction often led her to engage in compulsive behaviors, as she believed that keeping her mind busy was the only way to prevent the memories from overwhelming her. This downward comparison did little to alleviate her guilt but offered a fleeting sense of control. She believed these rituals were necessary, yet they only served to reinforce her negative self-perception. The more she relied on these strategies, the more she felt trapped in a cycle of guilt and fear, leading her to question her abilities as a mother, a wife, and a professional. Her attempts to manage the anxiety through these maladaptive strategies only served to distort her memories, making the traumatic event feel closer and more vivid, as though it was still happening rather than something from her past. Each time she resorted to these coping mechanisms, Aisha felt a silent confirmation that she was broken, leading her to internalize the idea that her worth was tied to her mistakes. The maladaptive strategies she employed reinforced her sense of threat, as she never allowed herself to experience situations that might prove safe, leaving her feeling constantly on edge and vulnerable. This avoidance, however, only reinforced her negative self-perception, as she often thought that if she were truly capable, she would not have to shy away from places that reminded her of the accident. As Aisha struggled with her memories, they began to feel like a double-edged sword. Whenever the vivid recollections of the accident surfaced, they were accompanied by a deep sense of shame, leading Aisha to conclude that these memories were proof of her inadequacy and inability to protect those around her. Once the memory had surfaced, it transformed her current reality into a state of threat, as she felt as though she was back at the construction site, reliving the chaos and horror all over again. The more she tried to push them away, the more they surfaced, often triggered by the mundane sounds of daily life. Each auditory recall — a hammer hitting a nail or the laughter of children playing outside — would send her spiraling back to that moment of chaos. In response to these distressing memories, Aisha turned to rituals as a form of self-protection, believing that by distracting herself, she could stave off the anxiety that threatened to overwhelm her. To cope, she learned to distract herself from these memories by engaging in rituals, believing that if she could just focus on how much worse the situation could have been, she could somehow lessen her anxiety. It became increasingly difficult for her to access the memory deliberately, yet when it did come unbidden, it was accompanied by sharp feelings of shame and self-recrimination. She felt as if she had lost a part of herself, and the person looking back in the mirror was someone she no longer recognized. Aisha's pervasive sense of threat was not limited to her environment; it seeped into her relationships, creating a barrier between her and her husband, who she felt could never understand the depths of her despair. This isolation only exacerbated her negative appraisals of herself. She would often think that if she were stronger or smarter, she could have prevented the accident. The cycle of negative thoughts and fears consumed her, each layer building upon the last. She believed that her actions had irrevocably changed her life and that she could never return to the person she once was. Finally, after months of grappling with these overwhelming feelings, Aisha reached a breaking point. One evening, while watching her children play, she felt a wave of despair wash over her. The joy she once felt in their laughter felt tainted by her guilt. It was in that moment of profound sadness that Aisha realized she could not continue to live in this self-imposed prison. Seeking help felt like a daunting step, but she knew she had to confront her fears and the memories that haunted her. Aisha hoped that therapy could help her reclaim the parts of herself she believed were lost, and perhaps, just perhaps, allow her to forgive herself for the mistake that had changed everything.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not convey how Aisha's negative appraisals influenced her maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."

  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."

  e.g. "When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible."
  e.g. "She had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed her body to settle enough to sleep, so she checked them twice."
  e.g. "The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong."

vignette_attempts.vignette: Aisha, a 47-year-old architect, had always prided herself on her ability to visualize spaces and design efficiently. However, one fateful afternoon, while overseeing a construction site, a tragic accident occurred. A miscalculation on her part led to a scaffolding collapse that seriously injured a worker. The event replayed in her mind like a relentless loop; she could taste the dust that filled the air and hear the distant cries for help, sensations that suddenly returned to her whenever she tried to recall the incident. This vivid recall left Aisha feeling not only horrified but also deeply ashamed. She often found herself ruminating on the blunder, believing that someone else in her position would have acted differently. This constant self-blame led Aisha to develop various mental rituals, convinced that if she performed them, she might prevent anything bad from happening again. Aisha’s belief that she was responsible for the accident drove her to engage in these maladaptive strategies, reinforcing her negative view of herself. Each time she resorted to her rituals, she felt a quiet confirmation that she was fragile, further entrenching her negative appraisals. Each time she engaged in these rituals, she could not shake the belief that her inability to cope without them confirmed her fragility, deepening her conviction that she was somehow less than others who navigated life more easily. Her belief that she was responsible for the accident drove her to engage in these maladaptive strategies, as she thought they would somehow absolve her guilt and protect her from further harm. The weight of her self-blame was heavy, and she felt unrecognizable as the confident architect she once was. In the months that followed, Aisha's world began to shrink. She distanced herself from her colleagues and avoided social gatherings, feeling isolated and set apart from others who seemed to navigate life effortlessly. Every time she heard a loud noise, a sudden laugh, or even the whir of machinery, she would jump, her heart racing as if she were still at the construction site. Aisha had come to believe her life was now fraught with danger, and she often acted as though she was still in immediate peril, even when she was at home, surrounded by her family. When faced with this overwhelming sense of threat, it seemed only sensible to her to avoid certain environments and situations that might trigger her anxiety, allowing her world to grow smaller and more contained. Her perception of danger felt so immediate that it led her to adopt avoidance strategies, as she thought steering clear of potential triggers was the only way to keep herself safe. The anxiety bled into her work, leaving her unable to concentrate on her designs or communicate effectively with her team. Each time she relied on these coping mechanisms, Aisha felt an unspoken message reinforcing that she was incapable of handling her responsibilities, deepening her negative self-perception. The resulting feelings of inadequacy would then spiral into a belief that she was a failure, which further fueled her anxiety and avoidance of professional interactions. Every time Aisha felt the need to employ these strategies, it left her with the insidious thought that her inability to cope without them confirmed her fragility, which only heightened the sense of threat she felt in her daily life.
